435.title: The born-free and the rest of us (1.19–1.22)
435.word: The born-free and the rest of us
435.hook: a few beings arrive at deep absorption by their very nature; for everyone else, Patanjali lists five things you need
435.howItsDone: Yoga teachers often present shraddha, virya, smriti, samadhi and prajna as qualities to cultivate over a lifetime, and encourage students that sincere intensity counts for more than natural gifts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samadhi with seed, absorption that still rests on something, and the kind that rests on nothing. With, without. What was your mind resting on? Today, who gets there, and how. Day four hundred thirty-five.

Every school has one. The kid who sits down at a piano at age four and just plays. The one who never studied and still aced the test. It's easy to look at them and think: well, that settles it, some people have it and I don't. Patanjali noticed that too, in his own way. In sutra 1.19 he admits that some beings reach a deep absorption by their very nature. And then, in 1.20, he turns to the rest of us, and doesn't sound worried at all.
screen: `THE KID WHO JUST PLAYS.` → `SOME HAVE IT, SOME DON'T?` → `PATANJALI TURNS TO THE REST OF US.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.19 names the born-free. For the bodiless ones and those merged in nature, the state arises from their very becoming, by birth, not effort. Who are they? The commentator Vyasa describes beings who have identified with the elements or with nature itself, and he adds a caution: their state looks like freedom, but it wears off, and they come back. So the born-free aren't the goal. They're a footnote. Sutra 1.20 is the main line. For everyone else, samadhi is preceded by five things: shraddha, faith, a settled trust that the path is real; virya, energy; smriti, memory, or mindfulness, keeping the aim in view; samadhi itself, the gathering; and prajna, wisdom. Notice that none of them is talent. They're all things you can grow. Then 1.21: it is near for those whose urgency is intense. And 1.22 adds a wry detail. Even among the intense, there's a difference: mild, medium and intense. So: mild intensity, medium intensity, intense intensity. Commentators work out nine grades from these. It sounds like a scoreboard, but read it the other way round. Patanjali is saying that how fast you go depends mostly on how much you care, not on what you were born with. Faith, energy, memory, gathering, wisdom. And then: how much do you want it?
screen: `THE BORN-FREE: BY NATURE.` · `THE REST: FIVE THINGS TO GROW.` · `NEAR FOR THE INTENSE.` · then, large: `MILD, MEDIUM, INTENSE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Let's touch the five, one at a time, a few breaths each. Faith: feel any trust you have that sitting like this is worth it. Energy: lengthen the spine a little, wake up the body. Memory: remind yourself why you came to this practice at all. Gathering: rest on the breath. Wisdom: notice, without judging, how intense your wanting is today, mild, medium or intense. All of them are fine starting points. The bell holds the time.
The born-free and the rest of us. A few reach absorption by nature; everyone else by faith, energy, memory, gathering and wisdom, at whatever intensity they bring.
screen: `THE BORN-FREE AND THE REST OF US — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: mild, medium, intense. Pick one thing you care about. Rate your effort today honestly, mild, medium or intense, and turn it up one notch for an hour. Day four hundred thirty-five.

pairs: memory: keeping the aim in view

myth: Vyasa treats the born-free as the goal of yoga
he says their state looks like freedom but wears off, and they return.
for everyone else, samadhi is preceded by faith, energy, memory, samadhi and wisdom
sutra 1.20.
Patanjali says the goal is near for those with intense urgency
sutra 1.21: tivra samvega.

fork.setup: you weren't born a natural meditator. according to Patanjali, what decides how near the goal is?
options: the intensity of your wanting and effort.
fork.reveal: 1.21 says it is near for those whose urgency is intense, and 1.22 grades even that: mild, medium, intense.

original.note: Sanskrit śraddhā: faith, trust. the first of the five that come before samadhi in 1.20.

trapdoor: what you thought: some people are just born spiritual.
what it means: a few are, by nature, and it's a detour; everyone else grows five qualities, at the intensity they choose.
what a scholar hears: 1.19 is bhava-pratyaya (by birth) for videhas and prakriti-layas; 1.20 is upaya-pratyaya (by means); commentators combine 1.21–1.22 into nine grades of practitioner.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.19–1.22 (the born-free; faith, energy, memory, samadhi, wisdom; mild, medium, intense)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.19 (the videhas and prakriti-layas return)

436.title: Or — devotion to Ishvara (1.23–1.26)
436.hook: after all the talk of effort and intensity, Patanjali adds one small word, or, and opens a second road
436.tomorrow: Om is his name; repeat it; know its meaning
436.howItsDone: Many Hindu yoga lineages treat ishvara pranidhana as central, practiced through prayer, offering one's actions to God, and repeating a divine name, while others teach it as one of several supports for meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the born-free and the rest of us, faith, energy, memory, gathering, wisdom, and the dial of mild, medium, intense. Did you turn one effort up a notch? Today, a different road. Day four hundred thirty-six.
screen: `THE BORN-FREE AND THE REST OF US.`

segments.voice: Sutra after sutra, Patanjali has been talking like a coach. Practice long, without breaks. Let go of thirst. Bring faith, energy, memory. Turn up the intensity. It's a lot of effort, and you might start to feel the weight of it. And then, in sutra 1.23, a tiny Sanskrit word, va. It means or. One syllable in either language, and it changes the whole tone. Or, the sutra says, there is another way.
screen: `PRACTICE. LET GO. TURN IT UP.` → `THEN ONE SMALL WORD.` → `VA: OR.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.23: ishvara pranidhanad va. Or, by devotion to Ishvara. Ishvara means the Lord. Pranidhana means placing yourself before, setting yourself down in front of, so devotion, surrender, dedication. The commentator Vyasa explains why this is a shortcut. Through this special devotion, he says, the Lord turns toward the practitioner and favors them, by his will alone, and absorption becomes near. So this road is not only your effort. It's met from the other side. Then Patanjali tells you who Ishvara is, in three short sutras. 1.24: a special kind of purusha, a special seer, untouched by afflictions, by actions, by their fruits and by the traces they leave. 1.25: in Ishvara, the seed of all-knowing is unsurpassed. 1.26: the teacher even of the most ancient teachers, because Ishvara is not limited by time. Notice what's not said. Ishvara here is not described as the creator of the world, and Patanjali doesn't name a particular god. Scholars debate how central Ishvara is to the whole text: some read the yoga of Patanjali as deeply theistic, others as a method in which devotion is one powerful option among several. Hindu teachers in many lineages take it as a real invitation to bhakti, the word you met at the end of the Shvetashvatara. Either way, the sutra is honest about something every tired practitioner learns: you don't have to do it all alone. Or.
screen: `VA: OR. A SECOND ROAD.` · `PRANIDHANA: SETTING YOURSELF DOWN BEFORE.` · `UNTOUCHED, ALL-KNOWING, THE FIRST TEACHER.` · then, large: `MET FROM THE OTHER SIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. For the first part of this sit, try hard: keep returning to the breath, alert, effortful. Then, halfway through, change the posture inside. Imagine setting yourself down in front of something greater than you, the way you'd set down a heavy bag. If you pray, place yourself before God as you know God. If not, place yourself before the stillness itself. Let the effort soften. Notice what changes. The bell holds the time.
Or. The small word va in sutra 1.23 that opens a second road: devotion to Ishvara, the Lord, who meets the practitioner from the other side.

Your line: the shortcut. Today, when something feels like it all depends on you, try the second road for one minute: set it down before something greater, and see what's still yours to do. Day four hundred thirty-six.

screen: `DAY 436 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: OM IS HIS NAME; REPEAT IT; KNOW ITS MEANING.`

pairs: teacher of the ancients, beyond time

myth: Patanjali describes Ishvara as the creator of the world
the sutras describe a special purusha, all-knowing and the first teacher, but not as creator.
Vyasa says the Lord favors the devoted practitioner
the Lord turns toward them and absorption becomes near.
pranidhana means setting yourself down before, devotion
placing yourself in front of the Lord: surrender, dedication.

fork.setup: you've practiced with all your effort, and you're worn out. sutra 1.23 offers something else. what?
options: devotion to Ishvara: a road met from the other side.
fork.reveal: or, by devotion to Ishvara. Vyasa says the Lord turns toward the devoted one, and absorption comes near.

original.note: Sanskrit īśvara: the Lord, the one who is able. in the Yoga Sutras, a special purusha, the first teacher.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'or' is just a connecting word.
what it means: a second road, devotion, beside effort and intensity.
what a scholar hears: Ishvara is defined as a purusha-vishesha, 'a special seer', not as creator; how theistic Patanjali's system is remains debated, and Vyasa reads 1.23 as grace (anugraha).

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.23–1.26 (devotion to Ishvara; who Ishvara is)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.23 (the Lord favors the devoted one)

437.title: Om is his name; repeat it; know its meaning (1.27–1.29)
437.hook: Patanjali gives the Lord of yesterday's sutra a name, and a three-part method for using it
437.howItsDone: Many Hindus repeat om or a divine name in japa, often on a mala of 108 beads, and teachers stress that the repetition should be joined with attention to the name's meaning, as Yoga Sutra 1.28 describes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: or, devotion to Ishvara, the shortcut, the road met from the other side. Did you set something down for a minute? Today the Lord gets a name. Day four hundred thirty-seven.

You've met om many times on this path. It opened year two, in the Chandogya, as the essence of essences. It was the bow in the Mundaka, the upper fire stick in the Shvetashvatara. So when Patanjali reaches it, you might expect a long hymn. Instead he gives it three sutras, crisp as a recipe. What om is. What to do with it. What happens when you do. Today, the recipe.
screen: `THE ESSENCE OF ESSENCES.` → `THE BOW. THE FIRE STICK.` → `NOW: A RECIPE.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.27: tasya vachakah pranavah. The word that expresses him is the pranava. Pranava is the old name for om, the humming syllable. Vachaka means the word that names, the expression. So om is to Ishvara as a name is to a person. The commentator Vyasa adds that the link between this word and what it names isn't made up by convention; it is already there, and using the word simply brings it to light. Sutra 1.28: taj japas tad artha bhavanam. Its repetition, and dwelling on its meaning. Two parts. Japa: saying it again and again. Artha bhavana: letting its meaning soak into you as you say it. Sound without meaning becomes noise. Meaning without the sound drifts into ideas. Together, they work. Sutra 1.29 tells you the result. From that comes inward-turned awareness, and the obstacles disappear. So the name does two jobs: it turns attention around, toward the seer, and it clears the road. Tomorrow you'll meet those obstacles, all nine of them. You practiced japa back in year one, with beads and a mantra. Here is one of its oldest textbook descriptions. And it's simple enough for anyone: one syllable, repeated, with the heart behind it. If om isn't your word, many Hindu teachers say the same method works with whatever divine name a person holds dear.
screen: `1.27: OM IS HIS NAME.` · `1.28: REPEAT IT, KNOW ITS MEANING.` · `1.29: THE MIND TURNS INWARD.` · then, large: `SOUND AND MEANING TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Sit upright and let the breath settle. On each out-breath, let om sound, aloud or silently, whichever feels right where you are. That's japa. Then, after a few rounds, add the second part: as you say it, let it carry some meaning for you. The Lord, the whole, the stillness, the one who sees. You don't need to define it. Just let the sound be full instead of empty. Again, and again. The bell holds the time.
Om is his name. Sutra 1.27: the pranava, om, is the word that expresses Ishvara. Repeat it and dwell on its meaning, and the mind turns inward.
Your line: japa, again. Three times today, at a red light, in a line, before a meal, say om silently, three times, and let it mean something each time. Day four hundred thirty-seven.

match.prompt: the om recipe, sutra by sutra.

myth: Patanjali says repeating om alone, without meaning, is enough
1.28 pairs repetition with dwelling on the meaning.
pranava is an old name for om
1.27: the pranava is the word that expresses Ishvara.
sutra 1.29 says the obstacles disappear
and awareness turns inward.

fork.setup: you've been chanting om for weeks, but it's become background noise. what does sutra 1.28 suggest?
options: join the sound with its meaning: dwell on what it names.
fork.reveal: taj japas tad artha bhavanam: its repetition, and dwelling on its meaning. the two belong together.

original.note: Sanskrit praṇava: an old name for om. in 1.27, the word that expresses Ishvara.

trapdoor: what you thought: om is a relaxing sound.
what it means: in the Yoga Sutras, the name of the Lord, to be repeated with its meaning held in mind.

what a scholar hears: Vyasa holds the bond between vachaka (the naming word) and vachya (the named) to be permanent, revealed rather than invented by convention, a view tied to Indian philosophy of language.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.27–1.29 (the pranava; japa and meaning; inward awareness)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.27 (the relation of word and meaning)
Chandogya Upanishad 1.1; Mundaka Upanishad 2.2.4; Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.14 (om in Block A)

438.title: The nine obstacles (1.30–1.31)
438.hook: Patanjali lists, nearly two thousand years ago, exactly what goes wrong when people try to practice
438.howItsDone: Yoga teachers often have students learn the nine antarayas by name, so that illness, doubt or a plateau can be recognized as a normal part of practice rather than a reason to quit.

segments.voice: Yesterday: om is his name. Repeat it, japa, again, and dwell on its meaning, and the obstacles disappear. Did om find its way into a red light or a queue? Today: which obstacles? Day four hundred thirty-eight.

Day one of a new habit: you're on fire. Day four: you have a cold. Day six: you're tired and skip it. Day nine: you wonder if any of this works. Day twelve: you had a great session, so you assume you've arrived, and stop paying attention. Day fifteen: the good feeling is gone and you can't get it back. Anyone who has tried to keep a practice knows this slide. Patanjali knew it too. In sutra 1.30 he names every step of it.
screen: `DAY ONE: ON FIRE.` → `A COLD. A SKIP. A DOUBT.` → `PATANJALI NAMES EVERY STEP.`

segments.voice: Here are the nine, from sutra 1.30. Vyadhi: illness. The body gets sick and practice stops. Styana: dullness, a mind that won't get going. Samshaya: doubt, is this even real? Pramada: carelessness, not tending the conditions. Alasya: laziness, heaviness of body and mind. Avirati: craving, the pull of the senses that won't let go. Bhranti darshana: false seeing, mistaking one thing for another, including mistaking a good moment for arrival. Alabdha bhumikatva: not reaching a stage, the plateau where nothing seems to move. And anavasthitatva: reaching a stage and failing to hold it. Patanjali calls these the scatterings of the mind. Then sutra 1.31 adds the companions that tend to show up with them, four signs you can feel in the body: pain, dejection, trembling of the limbs, and ragged breathing in and out. Two things stand out. First, how ordinary the list is. Illness and laziness sit right next to doubt and false seeing. The obstacles aren't demons. They're Tuesday. Second, the last two are about success, not failure: never getting to a new stage, and getting there and slipping off. Patanjali knows that a good day can be as much of a trap as a bad one. Naming them doesn't make them vanish. But it changes the story from I'm bad at this to oh, that's number three, doubt. And tomorrow's sutra gives the remedy.
screen: `ILLNESS, DULLNESS, DOUBT.` · `CARELESSNESS, LAZINESS, CRAVING.` · `FALSE SEEING, PLATEAUS, SLIPPING.` · then, large: `THE OBSTACLES ARE ORDINARY.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle on the breath. As you sit, watch for any of the nine as they show up. Dullness: a heavy fog. Doubt: a voice asking what's the point. Craving: a sudden thought of food or your phone. Each time you spot one, name it kindly, like spotting a bird: there's doubt. There's dullness. Then come back to the breath. Notice the body too: is the breath ragged, is there restlessness? Name it and return. The bell holds the time.
The nine obstacles. Illness, dullness, doubt, carelessness, laziness, craving, false seeing, failing to reach a stage, and failing to hold one: Patanjali's list of what scatters the mind.

Your line: disease, doubt, laziness and the rest. Today, when you stall on something that matters to you, name which obstacle it is, out of the nine, before you decide what to do. Day four hundred thirty-eight.

pairs: reaching a stage and not holding it

myth: Patanjali's obstacles are all moral failings
illness is the first one. the list is ordinary: body, mind and habit.
two of the nine are about what happens around success
never reaching a stage, and reaching one but not holding it.
sutra 1.31 lists signs in the body that come with the obstacles
pain, dejection, trembling of the limbs, and ragged breathing.

fork.setup: you had a wonderful sit yesterday, and today you assume you've arrived and stop paying attention. which obstacle is this, most likely?
options: false seeing: mistaking a good moment for arrival.
fork.reveal: bhranti darshana, false seeing: taking one thing for another. a good moment taken for the goal is a classic case, and the slipping that follows is the ninth obstacle.

original.note: Sanskrit antarāya: obstacle, literally what comes in between. Patanjali names nine.

trapdoor: what you thought: obstacles are bad luck or weakness.
what it means: nine ordinary ways the mind gets scattered, from illness to losing a stage you'd reached.
what a scholar hears: Vyasa calls the nine chitta-vikshepas, scatterings of the mind, and 1.31 adds four 'companions' (sahabhuvah): pain, dejection, trembling and disturbed breath.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.30 (the nine obstacles)
Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.31 (pain, dejection, trembling, disturbed breath)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.30 (the obstacles as distractions of the mind)

439.title: One-pointed practice removes them (1.32)
439.hook: nine obstacles, and Patanjali's remedy fits in one short sutra: practice on one thing
439.howItsDone: Many Hindu teachers advise choosing one practice, one mantra or one form of the divine and staying with it for years, rather than switching methods, and they often cite Yoga Sutra 1.32 for this.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the nine obstacles. Illness, dullness, doubt, carelessness, laziness, craving, false seeing, plateaus, slipping. Which one did you catch by name? Today, the remedy. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

A man needs water. He digs ten feet down in one corner of his field, finds only dry dirt, and gives up. He digs ten feet somewhere else. Dry again. By the end of the summer the field is full of shallow holes, and he's still carrying water up from the river. One hole, dug forty feet down, would have reached it. Yesterday Patanjali named nine obstacles. You might expect nine cures. He gives one, in a single short sutra, and it's that one deep hole: one thing.
screen: `TEN SHALLOW HOLES, NO WATER.` → `ONE HOLE, DUG DEEP.` → `NINE OBSTACLES, ONE REMEDY.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.32: tat pratishedhartham eka tattva abhyasah. To prevent them, practice on one principle. Tat, them: the obstacles. Pratishedha: keeping away, warding off. Eka: one. Tattva: a principle, a reality, literally thatness. Abhyasa: practice, the same word from five days ago, the steady return. So: to keep the scatterings away, return again and again to one thing. What is the one thing? Here the commentators part ways, and the sutra itself doesn't say. Vyasa reads it as any single object the mind is fixed on, one support instead of many. Others point to the sutras just before, about Ishvara and om, and read the one principle as the Lord. Both readings share the same shape: stop spreading out. The obstacles feed on scattering. Doubt grows when you keep switching methods. Laziness grows when nothing is the main thing. Plateaus feel endless when you keep starting over somewhere new. Vyasa also describes a mind that is one-pointed, ekagra, focused on a single object, and he treats it as the ground where real absorption becomes possible. That's where the word one-pointed in today's title comes from. Notice how modest this is. Not one perfect thing. Not the right thing. Just one thing, chosen and returned to. The next sutras, starting tomorrow, offer a list of possible one things. But today's teaching is simply the rule underneath them: pick one, and stay.
screen: `EKA TATTVA: ONE PRINCIPLE.` · `WHAT IS THE ONE THING?` · `OBSTACLES FEED ON SCATTERING.` · then, large: `PICK ONE, AND STAY.`

segments.voice: Before the bell, choose your one thing for this sit. The breath at the nostrils, a word like om, or the feeling of your hands resting. Just one. Now sit with it. Every time the mind offers you a second thing, a better object, a plan, a different technique, let it go and return to the one you chose. Don't switch, even if another seems more interesting. One thing, all the way to the bell. The bell holds the time.
One-pointed practice removes them. Sutra 1.32: to keep the obstacles away, practice on one principle, returning again and again to a single thing.
Your line: one thing. For one hour today, close every tab but one, literal or not, and give that one thing your full return, again and again. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

pairs: one-pointed: a mind on a single object

myth: Patanjali gives a separate cure for each of the nine obstacles
sutra 1.32 gives one remedy: practice on one principle.
commentators disagree about what the one principle is
Vyasa reads any single object; others read it as Ishvara, from the sutras just before.
the word abhyasa in 1.32 is the same practice word from 1.12
the steady return, paired earlier with non-attachment.

fork.setup: your meditation feels stuck, and you find three new techniques online. what does sutra 1.32 suggest?
options: pick one thing and keep returning to it.
fork.reveal: to ward off the obstacles, practice on one principle. switching keeps the mind scattered, which is what the obstacles feed on.

original.note: Sanskrit ekāgra: one-pointed, a mind fixed on a single object. Vyasa's term; the source of 'one-pointed'.

trapdoor: what you thought: one-pointed means intense concentration, forcing the mind still.
what it means: choosing one thing and returning to it, again and again, so the scattering has nothing to feed on.
what a scholar hears: Vyasa reads eka-tattva as a single object; other commentators read it as Ishvara, given 1.23–1.29; ekagra is one of Vyasa's five states of mind.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.32 (practice on one principle)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.1 and 1.32 (ekagra, the one-pointed mind)

440.title: Friendliness, compassion, joy, equanimity (1.33)
440.hook: one sutra gives four attitudes for four kinds of people, and says the mind grows clear by them
440.howItsDone: Many yoga teachers present sutra 1.33 as a daily practice for relationships, consciously meeting the happy with friendliness, the suffering with compassion, the good with gladness and wrongdoers with equanimity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: one thing. Pick one, and stay, because the obstacles feed on scattering. Did you close every tab but one for an hour? Today, Patanjali's first suggestion for what that one thing could be. Day four hundred forty.

Scroll through any feed for two minutes. A friend got engaged. A stranger lost their home in a flood. Someone you admire did something generous. Someone else did something cruel, and the comments are on fire. Four kinds of news, and each one tugs your mind a different way: envy, overwhelm, cynicism, rage. Most meditation advice starts inside your head. Sutra 1.33 starts out there, with other people, and with exactly those four kinds.
screen: `AN ENGAGEMENT. A FLOOD.` → `A KINDNESS. A CRUELTY.` → `FOUR TUGS ON THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.33 pairs four attitudes with four kinds of people. Maitri, friendliness, toward the happy. Karuna, compassion, toward those who suffer. Mudita, gladness, toward the good. And upeksha, equanimity, toward those who do wrong. By cultivating these, the sutra says, the mind becomes clear and settled. The Sanskrit for that is chitta prasadana, the mind made calm and bright, like water once the mud has settled. Look at how precise the pairing is. Friendliness toward the happy cuts envy at the root: their good news isn't your loss. Compassion toward the suffering keeps you from looking away. Gladness toward the good is harder than it sounds; it means being glad when someone else does right, without needing to be the one who did it. And equanimity toward wrongdoers doesn't mean approving. It means not letting their wrong take over your mind. Some modern teachers call these the four locks and the four keys: each kind of person a lock, each attitude the key that fits it. Buddhists know the same four qualities by another name, the brahma viharas, and practice them too. The Yoga Sutras place them right after one-pointed practice, as the first of several things the mind can rest on. So your one thing doesn't have to be the breath. It can be a way of meeting people.
screen: `FOUR PEOPLE, FOUR ATTITUDES.` · `CHITTA PRASADANA: THE MIND MADE CLEAR.` · `EQUANIMITY ISN'T APPROVAL.` · then, large: `THE FOUR KEYS.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone who's happy right now, and let a little friendliness toward them rise: good for you. Then someone who's suffering, and let compassion come: may this ease. Then someone who did something good, and let yourself be glad. Then, gently, someone who did wrong, and just let your mind stay level, not agreeing, not boiling. Then return to the breath, and notice how clear the water is. The bell holds the time.
Friendliness. Maitri, the first of the four attitudes in sutra 1.33, offered to the happy, alongside compassion, gladness and equanimity.
Your line: the four keys. Today, the next time news of someone tugs at you, ask which of the four people this is, and try the key that fits. Day four hundred forty.

match.prompt: the four keys, each to its lock.

myth: equanimity toward wrongdoers means approving of what they did
it means not letting their wrong take over your mind. approval isn't part of it.
the result of the four attitudes is chitta prasadana, a clear mind
the mind made calm and bright, like settled water.
Buddhists also practice these four qualities
they call them the brahma viharas.

fork.setup: a coworker gets the promotion you wanted, and they're thrilled. which key does sutra 1.33 hand you?
options: friendliness: their happiness isn't your loss.
fork.reveal: maitri, friendliness, is the attitude toward the happy. it cuts envy at the root.

original.note: Sanskrit maitrī: friendliness, goodwill; from mitra, friend. the first of the four attitudes in 1.33.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to everyone, the same way.
what it means: four different attitudes, each matched to a different kind of person, for the mind's own clarity.
what a scholar hears: maitri, karuna, mudita and upeksha match the Buddhist brahma viharas; in 1.33 their stated fruit is chitta prasadana, clarity of mind, not only ethics.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.33 (friendliness, compassion, gladness, equanimity)
the brahma viharas in Buddhist texts (e.g. Digha Nikaya 13)
the 'four locks and four keys' image (modern yoga teaching, e.g. Swami Satchidananda)

441.title: Or — the breath (1.34)
441.hook: the second door Patanjali offers into a clear mind is the one you're already walking through: the breath
441.tomorrow: or — a luminous object; or a sorrowless mind; or a great heart
441.howItsDone: Yoga teachers often introduce sutra 1.34 as a gentle lengthened exhale with a short pause, well before the fuller pranayama practices of the second chapter, and caution students never to strain the breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four keys. Friendliness for the happy, compassion for the suffering, gladness for the good, equanimity for the ones who do wrong. Did one key fit a lock? Today ends the week. Day four hundred forty-one.

Watch someone who's just received bad news. Before they say a word, they let out a long breath. Watch a basketball player at the free-throw line: one slow exhale, then the shot. Watch a child after crying: the shaky breaths, then a deep sigh, then quiet. Nobody taught them that. The body seems to know that a long breath out settles something. Sutra 1.34 is one line long, and it starts with the same small word you met on day four hundred thirty-six: or.
screen: `BAD NEWS: A LONG BREATH OUT.` → `THE FREE THROW: ONE EXHALE.` → `THE BODY ALREADY KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.34, in paraphrase: or, by breathing out and holding the breath. The words are prachchhardana, breathing out, almost expelling, and vidharana, holding, keeping it out. The sutra is in the middle of a list of ways to make the mind clear, which began yesterday with the four keys. Notice the va again, or. Patanjali isn't saying everyone must do this. He's saying here is another door. The commentator Vyasa reads it as a slow, controlled breathing out through the nostrils, then a pause before the next breath. Notice what it is not: it is not a big, straining hold, and it isn't the full breath discipline of the second chapter, which comes later in the book. It's simple and gentle: the out-breath lengthened, a pause at the bottom. Why does this help? The text doesn't explain, and it doesn't need to. You've seen it today in three scenes. A long breath out is something the body already uses to settle itself. Here it becomes a door for the mind. Now look back at the week. Day one, the born-free and the rest of us. Day two, or, devotion to Ishvara. Day three, om is his name. Day four, the nine obstacles. Day five, one thing. Day six, the four keys. And today: or, the breath. A week of doors, each one a way back to stillness.
screen: `PRACHCHHARDANA: BREATHING OUT.` · `VIDHARANA: A PAUSE, HOLDING OUT.` · `GENTLE, NOT STRAINED.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `A WEEK OF DOORS.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath be natural for a few rounds. Then let each out-breath grow a little longer than the in-breath, slow and easy, through the nose. At the bottom of the out-breath, rest for a moment, just a moment, before the next breath comes on its own. No forcing, no gasping. If you feel any strain, go back to normal breathing. Long out, a little pause, let it come in. The bell holds the time.
Or. In sutra 1.34, the second door to a clear mind: breathing out, and resting in the pause before the next breath.
Your line: or the breath. The next time your mind won't settle today, try the second door: one long breath out through the nose, and a small rest at the bottom. Day four hundred forty-one.

trapdoor: what you thought: breath work is advanced yoga.
what it means: one simple door: a long breath out, and a small pause.
what a scholar hears: 1.34 sits in a list of means to chitta prasadana (1.33–1.39); Vyasa glosses prachchhardana as expelling breath through the nostrils, and vidharana as keeping it out.
